passage: I'm Sangeeta, and I sat next to Sarika at the market research agency. Last quarter our client's campaign was underperforming. Our boss told Sarika to 'make the numbers look better' for the presentation, maybe by dropping the weakest cities. I saw her stop typing and stare at her screen for a long time. She went into the boss's cabin and came out twenty minutes later, looking tired. She presented all the cities, but added a slide showing where the campaign was working and a plan to fix the rest. The client was unhappy at first, then asked her to lead the fix. I don't know what she said to the boss. But I know I'd have been tempted to just drop those cities.

Week two: He read the company's privacy policy twice and asked his manager, Jasleen. She said clearly that patient data could not be used for sales. Vikas felt relieved, then worried the sales colleague would be annoyed.

passage: At 9 pm, with the client presentation at ten the next morning, Ramesh finished the campaign report and felt his stomach sink. Sign-ups were twenty per cent below target. His manager, Yamini, had told the client last week that they were 'on track'. She called from a cab. 'Can we count the newsletter subscribers as sign-ups? Just this once.' They weren't the same thing, and Ramesh knew the client would base next quarter's spending on these numbers. He took a breath. 'I can show both, clearly labelled, with a note on why sign-ups dipped and what we'd change. If we blur them, it'll come out later.' There was a long silence and traffic noise. 'Send me both slides,' she said. He worked till midnight on the explanation. The client was disappointed, but at the end asked Ramesh to join the next planning call.

qa.q: What made Ramesh's alternative honest and workable?

qa.q: How might the client have seen Ramesh after the meeting?

"Just drop weeks three and four," Saurabh said, leaning over Naveen's screen. "The server outage skewed them. Then the retention number looks right for the client."
Naveen scrolled. "If we drop them, retention goes from sixty-one to seventy-four percent."
"Exactly. Seventy-four is the real story."
"But the outage was ours. Customers left because of it. That's real too."
Saurabh straightened. "Are you saying I'm lying?"
"No." Naveen's mouth was dry. "I'm saying if the client finds out we removed two weeks without saying so, it'll look like we were hiding something."
"So what do you suggest?"
"Show both. Sixty-one overall, seventy-four without the outage weeks, with a footnote. And a line about what we fixed."
Saurabh was silent a while. "That's more honest. It's also longer."
"One footnote."
Saurabh sighed. "Fine. Draft to me by four."

qa.q: What would retention be if weeks three and four were dropped?
qa.a: Seventy-four percent.

qa.q: What was Naveen feeling when Saurabh asked 'Are you saying I'm lying?'
qa.a: Naveen felt nervous, mouth dry, but held firm about honest reporting.

qa.q: Why was Naveen's suggestion a good way to report honestly under pressure?
qa.a: Showing both figures with a footnote and what was fixed keeps the truth visible while still explaining the outage.

qa.q: How might Saurabh see the compromise?
qa.a: Saurabh feels challenged at first, but comes to see it as more honest, even if slightly longer.

grounding: A young analyst resists pressure to drop inconvenient weeks from a client metric and proposes transparent reporting.

passage: When the vendor list for our office renovation landed on my desk, I, Payal, saw my cousin Rafiq's interior firm on it. His quote was the lowest. Nobody at work knew we were related. For about ten minutes I told myself it didn't matter; the numbers were the numbers. Then I pictured someone finding out after I had approved it. Even if Rafiq's firm was the best choice, nobody would believe I had chosen fairly. So I walked to my manager's cabin and said, "I need to declare something. One of the vendors is my cousin. I should step out of this decision." She thanked me, noted it in the file, and gave the evaluation to a colleague. Rafiq was annoyed when I told him. "You could have helped me." "I did," I said. "Now if you win, nobody can say it was me." He won, as it happens. And I slept fine.

qa.q: Whose firm was on the vendor list?
qa.a: Payal's cousin Rafiq's interior firm.

qa.q: What was Payal feeling during the ten minutes of telling that it didn't matter?
qa.a: Payal felt tempted and uneasy, trying to believe the numbers settled it, until imagining being found out.

qa.q: Why was declaring the relationship right even if Rafiq's firm was best?
qa.a: It kept the decision fair and believable, so the choice could not be questioned later.

qa.q: How did Rafiq feel when Payal told him, and why?
qa.a: Rafiq was annoyed, hoping for help, and didn't see at first that stepping back protected his win from suspicion.

grounding: A young professional declares a conflict of interest with a relative's firm and steps out of the decision.

subtype: Conflict of Interest, Data Privacy & Honest Reporting
passage:
Thursday night

Karthik wants the investor deck to say "82,000 active users". I ran the numbers. 82,000 people signed up. 19,000 used the app more than once last month. "Active" means the second number. He knows that.

In the meeting he said, "Everyone rounds up, Zubin. We need this round." I didn't argue in front of the others. My face was hot and I just nodded, which I hate.

I've been walking around the flat for an hour.

Here's what I'm going to do. Tomorrow morning, before the deck goes out, I'll send Karthik a short email with both numbers, the exact definitions, and a line saying I can't put my name on "82,000 active". I'll offer a better story instead: the 19,000 are growing 15 percent a month. That's actually good.

If he still wants it, I'll take it to the co-founder.

Scared of losing this job. More scared of lying to people who give us money.

qa.q: How many people used the app more than once last month?
qa.a: 19,000 used the app more than once last month.

qa.q: What was Zubin feeling after nodding in the meeting?
qa.a: Zubin felt ashamed and anxious about going along silently, torn between fear of losing the job and fear of misleading investors.

qa.q: What makes Zubin's plan for the morning a wise one?
qa.a: Zubin puts both numbers and definitions in writing, refuses to sign off the false one, offers an honest positive story, and knows who to go to next.

qa.q: How might the investors be affected if the deck said "82,000 active users"?
qa.a: They would make decisions based on a misleading number and could feel betrayed later, damaging trust in the whole company.

grounding: A young analyst plans to report user numbers honestly and in writing when a manager pressures the team to inflate a metric.

passage:
The pathology lab on Station Road in Kottayam opens at seven, and Francis is usually alone at the front desk until eight.

On Tuesday a man in a white kurta came in, smiling, and leaned on the counter. "I'm from the ward councillor's office. Just tell me if Thomas from the bakery's sugar test came back high. He's standing in the co-operative election. People have a right to know."

Francis felt his neck go warm. The man was friendly, and the councillor's office paid for the lab's new signboard. "I'm sorry, I can't share anyone's reports," Francis said. "Only the patient or someone with his written permission."

"Just a yes or no."

"Not even that."

The man left without smiling. Francis wrote down the time and what was asked, and when Kavitha, the lab owner, arrived, he told her everything. She read the note, then locked the report cabinet and said, "Good. We'll write to the councillor ourselves."

qa.q: Whose test result did the man ask about?
qa.a: He asked about Thomas from the bakery's sugar test.

qa.q: How did Francis feel when the man pressed for "just a yes or no"?
qa.a: Francis felt uneasy and pressured, with his neck going warm, because the man was friendly and the councillor's office had helped the lab.

qa.q: What steps did Francis take that protected the patient?
qa.a: He refused to share even a yes or no, wrote down the time and request, and reported it to Kavitha the same morning.

qa.q: How might Thomas from the bakery feel if he learned about this request?
qa.a: Thomas would likely feel alarmed that someone tried to use his health information against him, and grateful that the lab kept it private.

grounding: A young lab worker refuses to disclose a patient's data under political pressure and reports the request honestly to his employer.

subtype: Conflict of Interest, Data Privacy & Honest Reporting
passage:
In Johannesburg, Zanele was preparing the quarterly report for a big retail client. The campaign had flopped: sales barely moved.
Her boss, Thabo, leaned over her desk. "Show the clicks, not the sales. Make it look like a success. They'll renew."
Zanele's stomach tightened. The clicks had come mostly from bots, which she'd flagged last month.
She took a breath. "If they find out later, we lose them and our name. Can I show what worked, what didn't, and what we'll change? I think honesty is how we keep them."
Thabo sighed. "And if they leave?"
"Then they leave trusting us. And they might come back."
He tapped the desk. "Show me both versions by five."
She did. He chose hers, with a line added about a new approach. The client didn't renew for six months. Then they came back with a smaller project.

qa.q: What did Thabo want the report to show?
qa.a: The clicks, not the sales.

qa.q: What was Zanele feeling when Thabo asked her to make it look like a success?
qa.a: Zanele felt uneasy and tense, her stomach tightening, knowing the clicks came mostly from bots.

qa.q: Which choice helped Zanele report honestly under pressure, and why?
qa.a: Offering an honest version with a plan, and showing both versions, let her refuse to mislead while giving Thabo a way to agree.

qa.q: How might the client have felt reading an honest report?
qa.a: The client might have been disappointed but also trusted the agency more, which is why they returned later.

grounding: Shows a young analyst resisting pressure to present misleading metrics and reporting honestly.

At the private hospital in Indore, Mridul managed the patient database. One afternoon his colleague Binita came to his desk. "My cousin works for a health-products company. Can you send me the list of diabetes patients with phone numbers? He just wants to share offers."
Mridul felt his face go warm. Binita was his friend; she'd covered for him when his father was ill.
"I can't," he said. "Patients gave us their data for treatment, not for sales calls. And it would be a conflict of interest for you too."
She looked annoyed. "Nobody would know."
"I would. And if patients found out, they'd stop trusting the hospital."
That evening he told the privacy officer about the request, without dramatics, and asked for access rules to be tightened. The next week the hospital sent a reminder to all staff. Binita was cold for a few days, then brought him tea.

qa.q: What did Binita ask Mridul to send?
qa.a: The list of diabetes patients with phone numbers.

qa.q: How did Mridul feel when Binita made the request?
qa.a: Mridul felt awkward and uncomfortable, his face going warm, because Binita was a friend who had helped him.

qa.q: What made Mridul's handling of the request both ethical and fair?
qa.a: He refused clearly with reasons, then reported the request calmly so rules could be tightened, without making it a personal attack.

qa.q: How might the patients have felt if their numbers had been shared?
qa.a: They would likely feel betrayed and exposed, since they gave their data only for treatment.

grounding: Illustrates a young professional protecting client data and handling a colleague's conflict of interest honestly.
